items.abstract: This chapter explains the assessment of boards and board committees, such as the corporate governance rules of the New York Stock Exchange that require boards of listed companies to conduct a self-evaluation at least annually. It clarifies that a board review should take a strategic perspective, considering the directors' ability to handle long-term issues and reflecting on recent experience in the short term. It also discusses how information for a board review is obtained from an analysis of board and board committee agendas, papers, and minutes, as well as from interviews with each officer and member of staff concerned. The chapter looks at corporate governance rating systems for companies, noting that a corporate governance rating from an independent and respected organization can reduce a company's cost of capital. It compares corporate governance assessment systems, which monitor and assess the overall level of corporate governance country by country.

items.abstract: <jats:p>This study utilizes stellar boards of directors as identified by Business Week and known to boost investor confidence and compares them to NASDAQ boards using an alternative governance assessment.  Specifically, the author examined board independence, over-commitment, size, perks, compensation, and other performance measures.  The author finds differences in these measures.  In particular, board independence, over-commitment, and size for some of the NASDAQ 100 differs from that of stellar boards in the presence of fewer connections to measures of performance.  These results suggest for the NASDAQ technology companies' specific ways to change the board of directors' operations and conduct to improve investor confidence.</jats:p>
title: Corporate Boards of Directors' Structure and Governance: How Does the NASDAQ 100 Stack Up Against Stellar Boards?
